claim: For Claude Fable 5.2 the recommended starting effort is high, the API default, and it should be tuned against the user's own evals rather than assumed.
why: Most of the capability gain is already present at high, and above it gains are uneven and task-dependent.
check: Look at the effort set for Fable 5.2 work in settings, skills and subagents; a blanket xhigh or max with no measured gain is a problem.
quote: Start at `high`, the default for Claude Fable 5.2 on the Claude API.

claim: An effort setting tuned on Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Opus 5.5 should not be carried over to Fable 5.2; the effort sweep should be rerun.
why: Effort levels rank the same across models but the amount of thinking at each level differs.
check: If a setup migrated to Fable 5.2 and kept old per-model effort values unchanged, flag it as unvalidated.
quote: So, rerun your effort sweep rather than carrying over a setting you tuned on Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Opus 5.5.

claim: Low effort on Fable 5.2 is the intended level for quick back-and-forth, well-specified tasks and high-volume work such as fast subagents.
why: On coding evaluations Fable 5.2 at low scored close to Fable 5.1 at higher effort.
check: Subagents doing routine, well-specified work that run at high or xhigh are candidates for low.
quote: `low` suits quick back-and-forth, well-specified tasks, and high-volume workloads (intelligent and fast subagents, for example).

claim: Medium effort fits interactive coding, chat and everyday knowledge work on Fable 5.2, while high fits hard coding, research, agentic work and long unattended runs.
why: The step from medium to high raised scores on most tracked evaluations but costs more tokens and time, so move down to medium wherever evals hold.
check: Check that interactive or routine work is not run at high or above by default without an eval showing the gain.
quote: `medium` suits interactive coding, chat, and everyday knowledge work.

claim: xhigh on Fable 5.2 is reserved for the hardest long-running coding and agentic work where a gain has been measured, and max is for measuring the ceiling or open-ended problems.
why: xhigh raised scores only slightly and used many more tokens; max is slower and uses many more tokens than xhigh.
check: A setup that sets xhigh or max globally, or for ordinary tasks, is overspending.
quote: `xhigh` is for your hardest long-running coding and agentic work where you’ve measured a gain.

claim: Max effort on Fable 5.2 runs slower and costs more than xhigh, often for only a small gain.
why: At max the model optimizes for capability without regard to token cost.
check: Look for max configured as a routine default.
quote: It runs slower and costs more than at `xhigh`, often for only a small gain.

claim: Fable 5.2 is more likely to end a turn early at low and medium effort, so agentic work at those levels needs the finish-the-whole-task prompt text.
why: Lower effort levels make the model more prone to stopping with a list of what remains, an offer to continue, or at an ordinary obstacle.
check: Agents run at low or medium on Fable 5.2 with no persistence instruction in the system prompt are likely to stop early.
quote: The model is more likely to stop early at lower effort levels.

claim: Anthropic gives a recommended system-prompt block, headed Finishing work, that tells Fable 5.2 to work through ordinary obstacles and leave deliberate blockers alone.
why: It addresses turns that end while work is still owed.
check: If an agent stops early, check whether a block like this is present and whether it keeps a confirmation step for risky actions.
quote: Please avoid stopping while you still owe work the user asked for. Be persistent and do not stop unless needed.

claim: In Anthropic's replay test the finishing-work text roughly halved unfinished sessions at medium effort but did not remove endings that list what remains and stop, and raised output tokens about 30 percent.
why: The text removes permission-asking endings but not list-and-stop endings, and the extra persistence costs tokens.
check: Do not expect the text to eliminate list-and-stop endings; budget about 30 percent more output tokens.
quote: It removed most endings that ask permission or offer to continue, but not endings that list what remains and then stop. Output tokens rose by about 30 percent.

claim: Because the finishing-work text makes Fable 5.2 ask less, the application must keep its own confirmation step for risky or irreversible actions.
why: The prompt does not remove the need for confirmation, but the model will ask less often.
check: Look for hooks or permission rules covering destructive actions when persistence prompts are used.
quote: Because the model asks less often with this text, keep your own confirmation step for risky or irreversible actions.

claim: Approval rules in a Fable 5.2 system prompt should name the exact actions to double-check, because a broad category made the model hold back about half of its routine messages to colleagues.
why: The model applies approval rules as written, including to routine actions.
check: Look for vague approval categories such as anything outside this conversation in instruction files.
quote: a rule that listed “sending messages to people outside this conversation” among the steps that need approval led the model to hold back about half of its routine requests to colleagues and other teams.

claim: To have Fable 5.2 improve code structure rather than only append to it, the prompt can state that the model owns and maintains the codebase.
why: Without an ownership statement the model tends to add to existing structure even when that duplicates code; with it, it consolidated duplicates in about 75 percent of runs versus under 10 percent.
check: For coding agents, check whether ownership is stated consistently with what the user wants (restructure versus minimal change).
quote: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you.

claim: The ownership sentence raised Fable 5.2 output tokens about 70 to 80 percent and led to unrequested changes, mostly new tests and documentation, sometimes altering existing behavior.
why: Owning the code makes the model make related fixes without being asked.
check: Where ownership text is present, check for review of diffs and for cost impact.
quote: With this prompt, output tokens rose by about 70 to 80 percent and the model made changes nobody had asked for, many of them new tests and documentation.

claim: A scope-limiting rule such as no drive-by refactors does not cancel the ownership sentence on Fable 5.2; the model still consolidated duplicated code in over half of runs.
why: The ownership statement outweighs an earlier restriction in the same prompt.
check: Where a user wants minimal diffs, make sure no ownership sentence is present anywhere in the instructions.
quote: A rule that limits scope doesn’t cancel it.

claim: Fable 5.2 closing PR summaries often omit small changes, so the diff must be reviewed alongside the summary.
why: The summary under-reports changes, especially under the ownership prompt.
check: Review workflows that trust the agent's summary without reading the diff are at risk.
quote: A closing PR summary from Claude Fable 5.2 often left out small changes, so review the reported diff and the summary.

claim: The migration guide gives a different ownership sentence and different figures than the prompting guide: This codebase is yours, with consolidation in about half of tries and about 1.5 times the output tokens.
why: The two official sources disagree on wording and on the measured effect (prompting guide: about 75 percent and 70 to 80 percent more tokens), so treat the numbers as indicative.
check: Do not cite one set of figures as definitive; note either wording is an Anthropic-suggested form.
quote: This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it.

claim: On Fable 5.2 the between-tool-call updates come back as thinking blocks that are empty by default, so a client that renders only text blocks looks silent during long agentic turns.
why: The default thinking.display is omitted; display updates or summarized returns the text.
check: For custom clients or SDK harnesses, check that display is set and thinking blocks are rendered; Claude Code manages this itself.
quote: So a client that renders only `text` blocks can look silent during a long agentic turn.

claim: A harness can count consecutive tool steps with nothing user-readable and append a turn-scoped system reminder, which roughly halved the longest silent stretch in Anthropic's test.
why: A reminder is cheaper than a standing prompt and leaves history append-only.
check: Where interactive users see silent runs, check whether such a reminder exists; reminders must be left in messages, not removed later.
quote: The user hasn't heard from you in a while: say in a few words what you're doing, then continue.

claim: A system-prompt line asking for an opening statement, brief updates and a standalone closing recap makes Fable 5.2 speak before its first tool call every time, at about 20 percent more output tokens.
why: It is intended where a human is directly in the loop.
check: Use only for interactive sessions; unattended pipelines gain nothing from the extra tokens.
quote: Before you start, say in a line what you're about to do; brief updates while you work help the user follow along.

claim: When the harness cannot add a reminder, a single sentence asking for a one-line update every few tool calls cut most long silent stretches on workflow-automation tasks.
why: It is the minimal fallback when no mid-conversation system messages exist.
check: Even with it, expect runs of several tool calls between updates.
quote: Every few tool calls, give the user a one-line update on where things stand.

claim: Anthropic recommends Fable 5.2 for long asynchronous work where nobody needs frequent updates.
why: The model works well on long-running asynchronous tasks but may stay quiet for several tool calls.
check: Fable 5.2 assigned to chat-like, update-hungry interactive work is a mismatch; unattended runs are a fit.
quote: Claude Fable 5.2 works well on long-running asynchronous tasks, so Anthropic recommends the model for work where nobody needs frequent updates.

claim: How much Fable 5.2 delegates depends on the harness: it rarely spawns subagents with a minimal tool, and delegates readily where prompts invite it.
why: Delegation follows prompt invitation, so standing delegate lines drive subagent count and cost.
check: Grep system prompts, skills and agent files for lines telling the model to delegate; review them first if subagents are many.
quote: If your system prompt, skills, or agent files tell the model to delegate, review those lines first.

claim: Subagents can be a large part of session cost, so the model each subagent runs on by default should be checked.
why: Delegation speeds parallel work but multiplies tokens, and Fable 5.2 is priced above Opus 5.5.
check: Verify subagent definitions set an explicit cheaper model where appropriate instead of inheriting Fable.
quote: However, subagents can account for a large part of what a session costs, so check which model your subagents use by default.

claim: If Fable 5.2 over-delegates, rewrite the subagent tool description to say what a subagent costs and when it is or is not worth it; a longer cost-focused description roughly halved subagent counts at high effort.
why: Cost information in the tool description restrains delegation better than a list of reasons to delegate.
check: Only worth doing where the harness already invites delegation; a plain description with no delegation prompts needs no change.
quote: In Anthropic’s testing at `high` effort, a longer description focused on this roughly halved the number of subagents compared to a shorter version.

claim: At xhigh and max Fable 5.2 was seen using subagents to review its own work, which Fable 5.1 did not do on the same tasks.
why: Higher effort adds self-review through delegation, raising cost.
check: At xhigh or max, expect extra subagent spend from self-review.
quote: At higher effort levels such as `xhigh` and `max`, Anthropic saw Claude Fable 5.2 use subagents in an agentic coding product to review its own work, which Claude Fable 5.1 didn’t do on the same tasks.

claim: Early testers had good results using Fable 5.2 as planner and orchestrator for other models.
why: The model pairs strong planning with delegation of parallelizable work.
check: A setup that runs Fable for every worker step instead of only planning is likely overspending.
quote: Early testers had good results with Claude Fable 5.2 as the planner and orchestrator for other models.

claim: Cautious notes can accumulate in memory and instruction files and Fable 5.2 follows them closely, producing unneeded approval requests, mostly in multi-agent setups.
why: The model treats carried-over instructions such as never retry as binding.
check: Audit memory files, notes and CLAUDE.md for stale cautions and absolute never rules.
quote: Memory can contain old instructions such as “never retry” that the model keeps following, so delete these instructions once they stop being relevant.

claim: For Fable 5.2, replace never rules with explicit exceptions, for example ask for approval before deleting files, if the model should retain responsibility for the action.
why: The model treats never as absolute.
check: Flag unscoped never or always rules in instruction files; they should state scope and the approval path.
quote: The model treats an instruction that contains “never” as absolute.

claim: A vague instruction to act more freely does not reduce approval requests on Fable 5.2; the routine steps that need no approval must be listed by name.
why: Naming steps raised unprompted retries from almost none to about half of tries in Anthropic's test; the general instruction changed nothing.
check: Look for instructions like be autonomous or act freely without a named list of permitted steps.
quote: a general instruction to act more freely changed nothing

claim: Stopping conditions such as stop and review at the first error can block autonomous Fable 5.2 work and should be removed or narrowed.
why: The model follows validation steps closely, so they halt otherwise unattended runs.
check: Check validation steps and reviewer-agent rules for blanket stop-on-error conditions.
quote: A condition such as “stop and review at the first error” can block autonomous work, so remove or narrow the stopping conditions that you don’t need.

claim: A token budget shown to the model in the prompt changes how much Fable 5.2 spends, and removing a large one lowered cost with equivalent performance at high and xhigh.
why: The budget size drives spending; the finding is about prompt text, not the API task budgets feature.
check: Look for harness text that shows remaining tokens to the model and test without it.
quote: In Anthropic’s testing on coding tasks at `high` and `xhigh` effort, removing a large budget lowered cost, with equivalent performance.

claim: The Opus 5.5 treat-that-answer-as-done chat lines reduce Fable 5.2 thinking on follow-ups and make it far less likely to flag mistakes in its earlier answers.
why: They shorten re-examination, which is where the model catches its own errors.
check: If instruction text carries those lines, remove them where self-correction matters.
quote: The model also became far less likely to point out mistakes in its earlier answers.

claim: A line such as answer directly without deliberating usually worked on Fable 5.1 but does not stop Fable 5.2 from thinking at medium and above; lower the effort level instead.
why: Fable 5.2 thinks before almost every reply at high and above, even to a greeting.
check: Find think-less instructions carried over from earlier models and replace with a lower effort setting.
quote: On Claude Fable 5.2, this addition doesn’t stop the model from thinking at `medium` and above. Remove such lines and lower the effort level

claim: Effort barely changes how long Fable 5.2 replies are, so reply length and tone must be controlled in the prompt.
why: Effort governs thinking and tool-call volume, not output length.
check: Do not accept lowering effort as a fix for verbose replies.
quote: Effort has little effect on the length of assistant turn responses. Use prompting to change the length and tone of replies.

claim: Hard style limits such as one instruction per sentence in 20 words or fewer are followed so closely by Fable 5.2 that prose becomes choppy.
why: The model follows style rules very literally.
check: Look for rigid sentence-length or format limits carried from earlier models and remove those no longer needed.
quote: a hard limit such as “one instruction per sentence, in 20 words or fewer” can make its prose choppy.

claim: For final reports and handoffs Anthropic suggests a Communicating clearly block telling Fable 5.2 to write for a low-context reader who has not seen the tool calls.
why: Readers of final reports after long agentic work usually have not seen the tool calls or files behind them.
check: Where users read handoff messages, check instruction text asks for self-contained reports with key points first.
quote: Write for an intelligent but low-context reader. The person reading has not seen your tool calls, your reasoning or the files you opened, and may be switching in from other work.

claim: Prompts, skills and tool descriptions that ask Fable 5.2 to write out its reasoning in the response should be removed, because they invite reasoning_extraction refusals.
why: The safety classifier declines requests to reproduce internal reasoning in response text; thinking summaries are available instead.
check: Grep instructions for show your reasoning or think step by step in the output.
quote: If your prompts, skills, or tool descriptions ask the model to write out its reasoning in the response, remove those instructions.

claim: Prompt or tool-description changes for Fable 5.2 should be made in new conversations, because editing system or tools in a stored conversation can fail the prefix check with a 400.
why: Thinking blocks are bound to the prefix that produced them.
check: Harnesses that resume stored conversations after changing system text or tools will see errors.
quote: Make these changes in new conversations only.

claim: On Fable 5.2 the history-editing check applies to every account, so custom harnesses that edit earlier turns can fail where they passed on Fable 5.1.
why: Fable 5.1 enforces only for newer accounts by default.
check: Custom harnesses that rewrite system, tools or earlier messages need the append-only check; Claude Code itself is unaffected.
quote: on Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the check is enforced for every account, whatever its age

claim: Nothing changes for users of Claude Code, claude.ai, Managed Agents or the Agent SDK regarding the Fable 5.2 prefix check.
why: These products build requests and keep the prefix intact.
check: Only code that builds its own messages array needs the append-only audit.
quote: Nothing changes for you if Claude Code, claude.ai,

claim: Moving a conversation from Fable 5.2 to any other model, including Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 or a fallback model, loses its reasoning for the turns that run there.
why: Thinking blocks are bound to the producing model and are dropped for models that cannot read them.
check: Routers or fallbacks that switch models mid-conversation incur re-planning cost on the first turn after the switch.
quote: loses their reasoning for the turns that run there.

claim: Fable 5.2 accepts only a Fable 5.2 or Mythos 5.2 advisor when it is the executor in the API advisor tool; any other advisor returns a 400.
why: The advisor must be at least as capable as the executor.
check: Advisor tool definitions pairing a Fable 5.2 executor with Fable 5.1 or Opus advisors are broken.
quote: A Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Mythos 5.2 executor accepts only Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Mythos 5.2 as its advisor.

claim: Fable 5.2 rejects forced tool use and any thinking configuration other than adaptive; use tool_choice auto with strict tool use instead.
why: Adaptive thinking is always on and forced tool_choice returns a 400.
check: Code or SDK calls that set tool_choice any or tool, or thinking disabled or budget_tokens, fail on Fable 5.2.
quote: Forced tool use isn’t supported.

claim: On Fable 5.2 the earlier computer_20251124 tool returns a 400 on every platform except Amazon Bedrock; the computer_toolset_20260801 toolset must be used.
why: Fable 5.2 supports computer use only through the new toolset.
check: Computer-use integrations declaring computer_20251124 need migration.
quote: A request to either model that declares a `computer_20251124` tool returns a 400 `invalid_request_error` on every platform except Amazon Bedrock.

claim: Safety-classifier refusals on Fable 5.2 may be retried on Opus 4.8 or Opus 5 only; those are the permitted fallback targets.
why: Fallbacks are limited to models that can serve the flagged category.
check: Explicit fallbacks lists naming other models are rejected.
quote: The permitted fallback targets for Claude Fable 5.2 are Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Opus 5.

claim: Fable 5.2 costs $8 input and $40 output per million tokens, down from $10 and $50 on Fable 5.1, with cache reads at $0.20.
why: Anthropic lowered the price with 5.2; it is still above Opus 5.5 at $4 and $20.
check: Cost estimates that use $10 and $50 for Fable 5.2 are out of date.
quote: $8 / $40 per MTok input / output (from $10 / $50), 5-minute cache writes $10, 1-hour cache writes $16, cache reads $0.20

claim: Anthropic says to start with the latest Opus model for most workloads and move to Fable 5.2 only when evals on Opus at higher effort still fall short.
why: Fable 5.2 is the most capable and most expensive generally available model.
check: Setups that default every task to Fable need an eval or justification showing Opus at higher effort fails.
quote: and move to Claude Fable 5.2 when your evals on a Claude Opus model at higher effort still don’t meet your requirements.

claim: Tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models.
why: Effort trades intelligence for latency and cost inside one model.
check: Before approving a model swap for cost, check whether lowering effort would meet the need.
quote: Tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models.

claim: The API default effort is high on Fable 5.2, Fable 5.1, Opus 5 and Sonnet 5.5, but medium on Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5.
why: Defaults differ by model, so a request that omits effort behaves differently across models.
check: Check that effort is set explicitly rather than assuming the same default across models.
quote: On Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, the default is `medium`; start there and adjust the same way.

claim: Multimodel strategies pair a lower-cost model with a frontier model so most tokens bill at the lower rate: an executor escalating to an advisor, or an orchestrator delegating bulk work to cheaper workers.
why: Most tokens are billed at the cheaper model's rate.
check: For setups running a frontier model on all turns, check whether either pattern would fit.
quote: an executor that escalates hard decisions to an advisor, and an orchestrator that delegates bulk work to lower-cost workers.

claim: Anthropic describes Fable 5.2 as its most capable model open to all customers, with Mythos 5.2 offering the same capabilities only to verified organizations.
why: Mythos access depends on Anthropic verification programs.
check: Do not assign Mythos IDs in a setup whose organization is not verified.
quote: **Claude Fable 5.2** (`claude-fable-5-2`) is Anthropic’s most capable model open to all customers.

claim: At low effort Haiku 5.5 is more likely to skip a search, stop early or skip a check in long agent prompts.
why: Lower effort reduces thoroughness in long agent prompts.
check: Haiku 5.5 subagents with long multistep prompts at low may need medium.
quote: In long agent prompts, the model is more likely to skip a search, stop early, or skip a check at `low`.

claim: Effort is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget, and affects all output tokens including tool calls and thinking.
why: Lower effort also gives fewer and terser tool calls.
check: Do not treat effort as a hard cost cap.
quote: Effort is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget.

claim: Changing top-level effort between requests can invalidate the prompt cache; vary it across workloads, or use per-message effort on supported models.
why: Top-level effort shapes the rendered prompt.
check: Custom harnesses that flip effort per turn without per-message effort lose cache hits.
quote: so vary it across workloads rather than within a conversation that relies on cache hits.

claim: On Opus 4.7, raise effort rather than prompting around shallow reasoning on complex problems.
why: Opus 4.7 respects effort levels strictly and scopes work to what was asked at lower levels.
check: Prompt text that tries to force deeper thinking on Opus 4.7 at low effort is misplaced.
quote: If you observe shallow reasoning on complex problems with Claude Opus 4.7, raise effort rather than prompting around it.

claim: In Claude Code no Fable model is the account default on any plan or provider; Fable 5.2 must be selected explicitly with /model fable or claude --model fable.
why: The default resolves to Opus 5.5 on most accounts.
check: A setup that expects Fable without selecting it is running on Opus 5.5.
quote: No Fable model is the account-type default on any plan or provider. Select one explicitly:

claim: The fable alias resolves to Fable 5.2 everywhere except Claude apps gateway sessions, where it resolves to Fable 5, unless ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL overrides it.
why: The alias tracks the Fable version Anthropic currently serves per provider.
check: Pinned deployments should set ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL rather than rely on the alias.
quote: Unless you set `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL`, the `fable` alias resolves to Fable 5 in

claim: The default model setting resolves to Opus 5.5 on Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, Enterprise and the Anthropic API.
why: Opus 5.5 is the current account-type default.
check: Do not assume Sonnet or an older Opus is the default.
quote: Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, Enterprise, and Anthropic API**: defaults to Opus 5.5

claim: Claude Code defaults Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 to medium effort, while the API default for Fable 5.2 and Sonnet 5.5 is high.
why: This is a direct disagreement between the Claude Code docs and the API docs, so the effective level depends on whether Claude Code sends effort.
check: Do not assume high for Fable 5.2 in Claude Code; check /effort status or whether CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL is auto.
quote: Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 default to `medium`, and Opus 4.7 defaults to `xhigh`.

claim: Claude Code resolves session effort in a fixed order: the CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL variable, then an in-session pick, then --effort, then saved settings, then the model default.
why: The environment variable outranks everything, including skill and subagent frontmatter.
check: If CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL is set, frontmatter effort and /effort have no effect.
quote: Claude Code resolves the session's effort level in this order, taking the first that applies:

claim: A skill's effort frontmatter overrides session effort until the end of the turn it runs in, or for the forked subagent's run when context is fork; a subagent's effort applies while it runs.
why: Frontmatter lets work-type-specific effort be set per skill or agent, subject to caps and the environment variable.
check: Check that heavy skills set effort in frontmatter rather than relying on the session level.
quote: A skill's `effort` applies until the end of the turn it runs in, or for the forked subagent's run with `context: fork`.

claim: A subagent with no effort of its own inherits the session effort only when it runs on the main conversation's model; on another model that level does not apply.
why: Effort scales are calibrated per model.
check: Subagents pinned to a different model should set effort in their definition.
quote: On another model, that level doesn't apply. To pick a subagent's level, set `effort` in its definition.

claim: Subagents that do not set a model inherit the main conversation's model at the time they start, so switching the session to Fable or Opus also runs delegated work there.
why: Claude Code resolves a subagent's model from the model the session is using.
check: Subagents for routine research or tests should set model in their definition to keep them on a cheaper model.
quote: To keep a custom subagent on a smaller model, set `model` in its definition.

claim: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL sets the default model for subagents, teammates and workflow agents not assigned a model another way; a definition's model field takes precedence.
why: It provides one place to put delegated work on a cheaper model.
check: Look for this variable in env settings when subagent cost matters.
quote: A per-invocation model or a definition's `model` field, including `inherit`, takes precedence.

claim: Claude Code sets the model by priority: /model in session, then --model, then ANTHROPIC_MODEL, then the model setting, then ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL.
why: Higher-priority sources outrank saved choices at each launch.
check: When a setup's model keeps reverting, check ANTHROPIC_MODEL in the shell and project or managed settings.
quote: You can configure your model in several ways, listed in order of priority:

claim: The opusplan alias uses Opus in plan mode and Sonnet in execution mode.
why: It pairs Opus reasoning for planning with Sonnet efficiency for implementation.
check: A reasonable cost-saving default for plan-then-implement workflows without Fable.
quote: This pairs Opus's reasoning for planning with Sonnet's efficiency for execution.

claim: Only the word ultrathink is a recognized keyword in Claude Code for one-turn deeper reasoning; phrases like think hard are ordinary prompt text.
why: Claude Code adds an in-context instruction and can raise the turn to xhigh for ultrathink only.
check: Instruction files that rely on think harder or think more as keywords are not doing anything special.
quote: Include `ultrathink` anywhere in your prompt to request deeper reasoning on that turn without changing your session effort setting.

claim: Claude Code docs say max effort may show diminishing returns and is prone to overthinking, so it should be tested before broad adoption.
why: Max is meant for hard problems left to run unattended.
check: Max set as a persistent default is a flag; in Claude Code max applies to the session only unless set via the environment variable.
quote: `max` may show diminishing returns and is prone to overthinking, so test before adopting it broadly

claim: For Fable in Claude Code, hand it the desired outcome and let it plan, rather than prescribing steps.
why: Fable investigates and verifies more than smaller models and sustains long sessions.
check: Prompts and skills that spell out step-by-step procedures for Fable are over-prescriptive.
quote: hand it the result you want and let it plan the path.

claim: The Claude Code docs say to skip verification reminders for Fable because it verifies its own work with less prompting.
why: Fable checks its work more often than smaller models.
check: This conflicts with the Fable 5.1 migration guide, which says to keep existing test-before-reporting instructions; check whether verification lines are kept or removed and apply the measured result.
quote: it verifies its own work with less prompting, so reminders to test or check are usually unnecessary.

claim: The Fable 5.1 migration guide says to keep prompts that ask the model to test or check its work before reporting, noting the Opus 5 advice to delete verification instructions does not apply, though it marks this as tentative.
why: It rests on a small number of reports; it conflicts with the Claude Code docs advice to skip verification reminders.
check: When auditing verification lines, treat removal as untested for Fable and prefer A/B evidence.
quote: If your existing prompt asks the model to test or check its work before reporting, **keep it** when migrating

claim: You cannot turn thinking off on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 or the Fable models in Claude Code; effort is the lever for how much they think.
why: These models use adaptive reasoning only, so alwaysThinkingEnabled false and MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 have no effect.
check: Settings that disable thinking to save cost on these models are inert; lower effort instead.
quote: You can't turn thinking off on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, or the Fable models.

claim: CLAUDE.md or the prompt can ask Claude to think more or less often within the effort level, and the model responds to that guidance within its effort setting.
why: Adaptive reasoning leaves room for prompt steering.
check: Compare with the Fable 5.2 finding that think-less lines do not work at medium and above.
quote: If you want Claude to think more or less often than the current level produces, you can say so directly in your prompt or in `CLAUDE.md`

claim: Content-based fallback from Fable models in Claude Code re-runs biology-flagged requests on Opus 5 and cybersecurity-flagged requests on Opus 4.8, and the session continues on the fallback model.
why: Safety classifiers flag cybersecurity and biology content.
check: Security or biology repos may drop sessions from Fable to Opus without the user noticing.
quote: biology-flagged requests re-run on Opus 5, and cybersecurity-flagged requests re-run on Opus 4.8.

claim: Fallback can trigger on the first request of a session because CLAUDE.md content and git status are in the request, so security material in the repo can trip the classifier.
why: The first request carries workspace context.
check: Use claude --safe-mode to test whether customizations trigger fallback.
quote: Fallback can trigger on the first request of a session, before you send anything unusual, because the first request carries workspace context such as your CLAUDE.md content and git status.

claim: On third-party providers model versions should be pinned with ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL variables, because aliases resolve to a built-in default that can lag or be unavailable.
why: Without pinning, users may be moved to older models or requests fail.
check: Bedrock, Foundry or Agent Platform deployments without pinned model variables are a risk.
quote: Set the model environment variables to specific version IDs as part of your initial setup.

claim: Fast mode makes supported models up to 2.5 times faster at higher per-token cost and is supported on Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 on the Anthropic API, not on Sonnet or Haiku.
why: It uses the same model with an API configuration that prioritizes speed.
check: Fast mode is for interactive latency; it is wrong for batch, CI or long autonomous tasks.
quote: Fast mode is a high-speed configuration for supported models, making the model up to 2.5x faster at a higher cost per token.

claim: Standard mode is better than fast mode for long autonomous tasks, batch or CI/CD pipelines and cost-sensitive work; fast mode suits rapid iteration and live debugging.
why: Fast mode trades cost for latency.
check: Check fastMode settings in pipelines and background sessions.
quote: Fast mode is best for interactive work where response latency matters more than cost:

claim: Enabling fast mode mid-conversation charges the full fast uncached input price for the whole context, and fast and standard keep separate caches, so it is cheapest to enable at session start.
why: Switching speed re-reads the conversation uncached.
check: Toggling /fast repeatedly in long sessions is costly.
quote: The first time you enable fast mode in a conversation, you pay the full fast mode uncached input token price for the entire conversation context.

claim: The fastMode setting alone does not enable fast mode on Fable 5.2; /fast must be run while using Fable 5.2, and persistence applies only if enabled while on Fable 5.2.
why: Fast mode preference is tied to the model it was turned on with.
check: A settings file with fastMode true and a Fable default will not run fast.
quote: On Fable 5.2, that setting alone has no effect until you run `/fast` while using Fable 5.2.

claim: On subscription plans fast mode is billed only through usage credits and not covered by plan rate limits.
why: Fast usage draws from credits even if plan usage remains.
check: Setups enabling fast mode broadly on subscriptions generate credit spend.
quote: For Claude Code users on subscription plans (Pro/Max/Ultra/Team/Enterprise), fast mode is available via usage credits only and not included in the subscription rate limits.

claim: Setting fastModePerSessionOptIn to true makes every session start with fast mode off, which helps control cost where users run many concurrent sessions.
why: By default a turned-on fast mode persists across sessions.
check: Managed settings for cost-sensitive teams should consider this key.
quote: This is useful for controlling costs in organizations where users run multiple concurrent sessions.

claim: The advisor tool pairs a cheaper main model with a stronger advisor consulted at decision points, and fits long multistep tasks where plan quality matters, not short tasks or work needing the strongest model every turn.
why: The advisor reads the full conversation but is called only at key moments.
check: Advisor use on short tasks adds tokens with little benefit.
quote: It adds less value on short tasks where there is little to plan, or on work where every turn needs the strongest model.

claim: In Claude Code the advisor must rank at or above the main model, so a Fable 5.2 main model accepts only a Fable 5.2 advisor.
why: Claude Code ranks models by capability for the advisor role.
check: An advisorModel lower than the main model is silently not attached.
quote: Claude Code ranks models by capability for the advisor role, and an advisor must rank at or above your session's main model.

claim: There is no setting to force or cap advisor calls; Claude decides when to consult, and prompt instructions are the only way to ask for more or fewer consultations.
why: Timing is model-driven rather than rule-based.
check: Instruction text such as consult the advisor before declaring done is the supported lever.
quote: There is no setting to cap or force advisor calls; if you want Claude to consult more or less often during a task, say so in your instructions.

claim: Pairing a faster main model with a stronger advisor typically costs less than running the stronger model throughout, and enabling the advisor does not invalidate the main prompt cache.
why: The advisor is called at decision points, but each advisor call re-reads the full transcript uncached.
check: Advisor use is cost-reasonable on long routine-heavy tasks.
quote: Claude calls the advisor at decision points rather than on every turn, so pairing a faster main model with a stronger advisor typically costs less than running the stronger model throughout.

claim: Subagents inherit the configured advisor and apply the pairing check against their own model.
why: Pairing validity depends on each model.
check: Subagents on a stronger or weaker model than the main session may or may not use the advisor.
quote: Subagents inherit the configured advisor and apply the same pairing check against their own model.

claim: The Fable 5.1 migration guide says prompts and skills written for earlier models are often too prescriptive and reduce output quality, so step-by-step scaffolding should be A/B tested away.
why: Fable 5.1 does better given a goal and constraints than enumerated steps.
check: Look for long numbered procedures in skills and prompts written for older models.
quote: Prompts and skills written for prior models are often too prescriptive for Claude Fable 5.1 and *reduce* output quality.

claim: Fable 5.1 reverses the older chat tendency: it uses less bold, fewer headers and lists, so anti-formatting language carried over from earlier models should be removed or made conditional.
why: Old over-formatting guardrails now over-correct.
check: Search instruction files for never use bullets or markdown rules aimed at earlier models.
quote: If the prompt contains anti-formatting language, remove it

claim: Fable 5.1 can show context anxiety in very long sessions, most often when the harness shows a remaining-token countdown, so context-budget counts should not be shown to it.
why: It may suggest a new session or trim its own work.
check: Check harness text or hooks that display remaining context to the model.
quote: In very long sessions it can worry about running out of context - suggesting a new session or trimming its own work - most often when the harness surfaces a remaining-token countdown.

claim: Fable 5.1 sometimes takes unrequested adjacent actions; the guide recommends stating that when the user is only describing a problem, the deliverable is an assessment and no fix should be applied.
why: It otherwise acts on adjacent steps such as composing emails or creating backup branches.
check: Agents that edit when asked only for analysis need explicit boundary text.
quote: When the user is describing a problem, asking a question, or thinking out loud rather than requesting a change, the deliverable is your assessment.

claim: Fable 5.1 progress claims on long runs should be audited against tool results, which in testing nearly eliminated fabricated status reports.
why: Long unattended runs can report unverified progress.
check: Autonomous-run prompts should require evidence for progress claims.
quote: Before reporting progress, audit each claim against a tool result from this session.

claim: For Fable 5.1 the guide advises using sub-agents frequently with guidance on when to delegate, instead of the earlier guardrail of suppressing delegation, and preferring asynchronous sub-agents over spawn-and-block.
why: Parallel sub-agents are dependable on 5.1 and long-lived agents keep their context; note Fable 5.2 guidance instead warns about over-delegation and subagent cost.
check: Standing delegation instructions written for 5.1 should be re-checked when moving to 5.2.
quote: Parallel sub-agents are dependable on Claude Fable 5.1 - instead of suppressing delegation (a common prior-model guardrail), use sub-agents frequently

claim: At xhigh and max on Fable 5.1, long deliverables may be drafted in thinking and written again, roughly doubling output tokens; the fix is to run them at high.
why: The model thinks more before writing at higher effort.
check: Large document or file generation at xhigh or max doubles cost without improving results.
quote: a longer wait and roughly double the output tokens.

claim: At low effort Fable 5.1 searches less and answers from memory more, especially for names of fast-moving products, so raise effort for those turns or add a verify-the-name instruction.
why: Low effort reduces search triggering.
check: Search-dependent low-effort agents need a search-first line or higher effort.
quote: At `low` effort, Claude Fable 5.1 calls a search or retrieval tool less often than Claude Fable 5 and answers from memory more

claim: Fable 5.1 is more likely to rewrite a whole file where a targeted edit would do, which a prompt line asking for surgical edits restores.
why: Whole-file rewrites cost output tokens and time.
check: For coding agents on Fable 5.1, check for a targeted-edit instruction.
quote: Claude Fable 5.1 is more likely than Claude Fable 5 to rewrite an entire file where a targeted edit would do

claim: Compared with Opus 5.5, Fable 5.2 differs in default effort (high versus medium), price ($8/$40 versus $4/$20), a 30-day data retention requirement and its history-editing check on every account.
why: A request omitting effort runs one level higher on Fable 5.2 than on Opus 5.5.
check: Moving a task from Opus 5.5 to Fable 5.2 changes cost and effort; set effort explicitly.
quote: the default effort is `high`, not `medium`, so a request that omits `effort` runs one level higher - set it explicitly

claim: Instructions to think less can make a Fable 5.2 request with a small max_tokens stop after a thinking block with no text, because thinking tokens count toward max_tokens.
why: The model keeps thinking at medium and above even when told not to.
check: Calls with small max_tokens relying on think-less lines need a larger max_tokens or lower effort.
quote: because thinking tokens count toward `max_tokens`: raise `max_tokens` or choose a lower effort level.

claim: Cache reads cost 2.5 percent of base input on Fable 5.2 and Fable 5.1, versus 5 percent on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 and 10 percent on other models.
why: Cheap cache reads make keeping the cache warm more valuable on Fable.
check: Cost audits for Fable should weigh cache hit rate heavily.
quote: prompt cache reads cost 10% of the base input price (2.5% on Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Fable 5.1, 5% on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5)

claim: Fable 5.2 has a 1M token context window, 128K max output, and always-on adaptive thinking, with effort controlling thinking depth.
why: Thinking cannot be disabled, so effort is the lever.
check: Settings that assume a 200K window or toggleable thinking for Fable 5.2 are outdated.
quote: Adaptive thinking lets the model decide how much to think, steered by effort.
